title: Type Coercion and Loose Comparison Bypasses
platform_conditions: ECMAScript 2020 semantics in Node.js runtime and browsers; identical coercion rules in both (Abstract Equality Comparison)
security_mechanism: The == operator applies ToPrimitive/ToNumber coercion before comparison, so values of different types can compare equal: '' == 0, '0' == false, [1] == 1, and document.cookie or query values parsed out of a string arrive as strings that coerce against numbers. On an authorization path, a check like value == 1 accepts '1', ' 1', or [1]. Query-string parsers that decode a[]=1 produce arrays where the code expects a string, and parseInt('08abc') stops at the first non-digit, so a validated-looking prefix hides the rest. Integers beyond 2^53 lose precision in doubles, letting two distinct 64-bit IDs collapse to one compared value.

source_sink_clues.source: Query strings, request bodies, cookies, and headers -- always strings or parser-produced arrays -- that flow into comparison or validation expressions.
source_sink_clues.sink: == / != on security-decision values; truthiness checks over parser-produced arrays; parseInt / Number validation feeding authorization; == on 64-bit identifiers

tracking_guards: Check security comparisons use === / !==, that expected types are asserted (typeof) before the check, that token/MAC comparisons use crypto.timingSafeEqual over equal-length buffers, and that large IDs stay strings or BigInt end to end.
not_candidate_when: Both operands are provably the same type by construction and the comparison uses ===, the compared value is a constant not derived from request data, or the check is non-security and coercion is the intended behavior.
